text: protest, the leather of the robe sticking slightly with each motion, heavier than usual. Weighted. Trapping warmth instead of wicking it off like normal. He winced. The outfit was fantastic for blending in with the shadows, both flexible and breathable, but it was heavy at the best of times. Right now, it sat heavier on him than he remembered. Every seam had absorbed something. The underlayer clung. He'd been carrying the extra weight long enough that he'd stopped registering it consciously, which probably explained why his back had opinions that it was only now getting around to voicing. He'd peel it off later, hang it up, let it dry properly. Later problem. He glanced down at his phone, adjusting his grip, and the faint glow of the screen caught the air around his hands. No fog. Not the building's water-thick atmosphere — that was everywhere, unavoidable, a permanent feature of the evening. His fog. The particular dark that clung to him when he didn't want to be seen, that softened his edges and swallowed his silhouette and had been as automatic as breathing since the first trial. It was just there. It was always just there. He turned his hand over slowly in the phone's light. Nothing. Just his hand. Just air. No shimmer of stealth, no ripple of distortion, no indication he had been cloaked at all, really. And come to think of it... he had no idea how long he’d even been fully visible for. Had he been uncloaked this whole time? He looked up at the group — really looked, the lens forgotten — and did the math with the particular speed of someone who had spent years reading rooms for a living. Orela's flashlight had swept this hallway. Multiple times. He'd been sitting on a toppled cabinet in the open, phone out, knife visible, not eight meters away, and not one of them had so much as flinched in his direction. “...Huh.” How did the others not feel him there? Was his terror radius even active? He reached inward for the low constant pulse of it, the thing that kept prey at the right edge of awareness. The thing that had always been there. The silence where it should have been was very loud. Across the hallway, Dwight was still against his wall. Still counting. Still wearing that expression — hollowed out, fraying at the edges, the look of someone standing at the threshold of understanding something they didn't want to understand. Danny looked at him for a long moment. No stealth. No presence. No terror radius. “...Wait.” The school flinched inward. All at once, simultaneously, every seam in the building giving up the pretense at the same moment — as if it had been holding its breath since the trial started and had finally, finally found its cue. The pipes went first. Not a chain reaction building from a source — all of them, the entire network detonating in the same instant with a shriek of pressure that compressed the air and hit the ears like a physical thing. Locker doors flew open along the hallway's length, torn off their hinges by the force of what came through them, water exploding outward in solid jets that crossed the corridor and hit the opposite wall hard enough to strip paint. Some doors didn't open at all — they shattered, the metal folding outward in jagged petals as the water behind them stopped asking permission. Ceiling tiles buckled and dropped, each one releasing its own small waterfall that joined the roar before it hit the floor, the sound building on itself until it stopped being individual sources and became a single deafening presence that swallowed everything inside it. The surge scattered the survivors across the flooded foyer, drowning out their yells beneath its violent crescendo, consuming the survivor’s panicked screaming shouts, and dousing them in spray from all sides. Orela's flashlight became a liability. The beam swung wild as the first jets hit — catching nothing useful, just strobing across walls and water and the shapes of people staggering, the light more disorienting than the dark had been. She swept it hard left, trying to find something solid to orient by, and a pressure wave caught her from the right and took her feet. The beam lurched toward the ceiling. Her shoulder hit something — a locker, a wall, she couldn't tell — before Leon's arm came across her chest and pulled, hauling her back against him and turning his body into a windbreak between her and the spray. She got a hand against the wall. Held. Across the foyer, Jake moved on reflex. He'd seen Dwight's legs go the instant the first wave hit — no purchase, no warning, just a man with too much height and not enough weight suddenly at the mercy of a current that had been waiting for exactly this. Jake was already moving when Dwight started to go down, closing the distance in two lurching strides, catching him by the arm and driving him hard into the nearest corner. He planted himself between Dwight and the worst of it, braced wide, and held. At the door, David had nowhere to go. The door was at his back — immovable, indifferent, the same door that had absorbed everything they'd thrown at it all night — and the water was at his front, coming in from three directions at once. He got his arm up, elbow leading, and turned his face into his shoulder as a jet caught him across the chest and drove the breath out of him. The force of it ground him back against the wood. He pushed into it, found his footing, lost it, found it again. Another wave hit, lower, and the cold of it surged up his torso. He coughed hard into his own arm and kept his feet. Down the hall, Danny was torn loose. No warning, no build — one moment he was sitting upright
